content: Angiostrongylus cantonensis is the primary causative agent of infectious eosinophilic meningitis. The inflammation and exacerbation of meningitis symptoms are primarily due to the presence of dead larvae of this parasite. Corticosteroids, such as prednisolone, are pharmacological agents used to mitigate the inflammation caused by this condition. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of corticosteroids in the treatment of eosinophilic meningitis. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, LILACS, and CINAHL, covering a wide range of publication years up to December 2014. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing corticosteroids with placebo for this condition. Two independent reviewers systematically collected and extracted data from the studies. The methodological quality of the RCTs was assessed, and the outcomes, as well as adverse effects, were analyzed. In this 2014 update, no new trials were identified for inclusion or exclusion. However, one RCT involving 110 participants (55 in the corticosteroid group and 55 in the placebo group) met the inclusion criteria. The study demonstrated that prednisolone significantly reduced the median time to headache resolution, with the treatment group experiencing relief in five days compared to 13 days in the control group (P < 0.0001). Additionally, fewer participants in the corticosteroid group reported persistent headaches after two weeks of treatment (9.1% versus 45.5%, P < 0.0001). The need for repeat lumbar punctures was also lower in the corticosteroid group (12.7% versus 40%, P = 0.002). Furthermore, the median duration of analgesic use was reduced in participants receiving corticosteroids (10.5 days versus 25.0 days, P = 0.038). Importantly, no adverse effects associated with prednisolone were reported in the treatment group. The authors concluded that corticosteroids, particularly prednisolone, are effective in alleviating headaches in patients with eosinophilic meningitis who report a pain score of four or higher on a visual analogue scale. However, the evidence supporting this conclusion is based on a single RCT, which had limitations in terms of allocation concealment and stratification. As a result, the study was graded as moderate in quality. The authors emphasized the need for future well-designed RCTs to further validate these findings.
